📚 Today you learned

Average True Range (ATR) as a Stop-Placement Tool

ATR measures a stock's average daily trading range over a lookback period (usually 14 days) — how much it typically moves, up or down, in a single session. It's a volatility ruler, not a directional signal. The practical use: instead of picking a stop level off a round number or gut feel, set it at 1.5-2x ATR below entry (or below the nearest structural support, whichever is wider) so normal daily noise doesn't shake you out. Today's GOOG search returned three different "support" numbers ($325-330 zone, $338-349 moving averages, $353-338 mean-reversion levels) because different methods measure different things — ATR tells you how much room a stock actually needs before a move means something. A mega-cap like GOOG typically runs a 2-2.5% daily ATR, so a stop 5-8% below entry is "normal," not "wide." SPXC's smaller, choppier range (conflicting $204-259 vs $213-259 readings from two sources today) is a textbook case of a name with a wider ATR relative to price — which is exactly why its stop sits further from entry than GOOG's does, proportionally.

Also today: Whipsaw — getting stopped out by normal volatility right before the stock reverses in your favor; the main failure mode ATR-based stops are designed to prevent.
